title: Plotting with the grammar of graphics

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
ggplot(), from the ggplot2 package, starts a plot from a data frame and a set of aesthetic mappings. An aesthetic mapping, made with aes(), says which column of the data controls which visual property of the marks: position along x, position along y, colour, and others. A geom is the kind of mark that represents each observation or group, and each geom_ function adds one layer of marks. Layers are added to the plot with +.

The function geom_histogram() divides the x axis into bins and draws a bar whose height is the count of observations in each bin. Unless told otherwise it uses 30 bins. A value on the edge between two bins is then counted in the lower bin. The arguments binwidth, boundary and closed set the width of the bins, where an edge falls, and which edge a bin includes.

The function geom_boxplot() draws the median and a box from the first to the third quartile. Its whiskers reach the furthest values within 1.5 times the interquartile range beyond each end of the box (below the first quartile, above the third). Values beyond the whiskers are drawn one by one.

A visual property written inside aes() is mapped: it varies with a column. Written outside aes(), as an argument of the geom, it is set: one fixed value for every mark. The function facet_wrap() draws one panel for each value of a column. The function ggsave() writes a plot to a file, at a size you give.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
A plot in ggplot2 is built from three parts.

The data: a data frame, one row per observation, as every section since tidy data has used.

The mappings: which column goes where. You write these inside aes(), short for aesthetics, the visual properties of a mark.

The geom: what kind of mark. Points for a scatter plot, bars for a histogram or a count, boxes for a boxplot.

You join the parts with +.

Two traps come up early. Inside aes() means “let this vary with a column”. Outside it means “make every mark this”. Write colour = "blue" inside and ggplot2 treats “blue” as data. And a histogram’s bars depend on bins you did not choose unless you choose them: set their width and where they start.

Save it to output/ with ggsave(), from the script, at a size you write down. Never export it with the mouse.

blocks.alt: A bar chart of eight body-mass bins: 9, 62, 94, 59, 51, 34, 29 and 4 penguins, from 2500 to under 3000 g up to 6000 to under 6500 g.
blocks.caption: The counts behind the histogram of penguin body mass with its bins chosen in code: 500 g wide from 2500 g, each including its left edge. The tallest bin, 3500 to under 4000 g, holds 94 of the 342 penguins with a body mass. The same counts are what the code writes to output/ beside the figure.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with a histogram of penguin body mass. Load the packages, read the file, and make the short columns used in the summaries section.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins <- penguins_raw |>
  mutate(
    species = case_when(
      Species == "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)" ~ "Adelie",
      Species == "Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)" ~ "Chinstrap",
      Species == "Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)" ~ "Gentoo"
    ),
    body_mass_g = `Body Mass (g)`,
    flipper_mm = `Flipper Length (mm)`
  )

range(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 2700 6300

Now the plot: the data, one mapping, one geom.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram()
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value with `binwidth`.
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing non-finite values (`stat_bin()`).

A histogram appears, and R prints two lines. Read both. The first says ggplot2 used 30 bins because you did not choose any. Thirty is not a property of penguins. It is a default, and the help page calls it “not a good default”. The second says 2 rows were removed: the two penguins with no body mass. The figure shows 342 penguins, and nothing on it says so.

Choose the bins. Body masses run from 2700 g to 6300 g, so bins 500 g wide, starting at 2500 g, cover them in eight bars. Say also which edge a bin includes. By default a penguin of exactly 3000 g goes in the bin “2500 to 3000”. closed = "left" makes each bin run from its left edge up to just under its right edge, so the same penguin counts in “3000 to under 3500”; the last bin also keeps its right edge.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 500, boundary = 2500, closed = "left")
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing non-finite values (`stat_bin()`).

The warning about the 2 removed rows stays, and it should. Now count the same bins yourself, so the numbers behind the bars exist somewhere other than in a picture. Dividing by 500, rounding down with floor() and multiplying by 500 gives each penguin’s bin start. count() can make the column it counts; the name goes on the left of =.

mass_bins <- penguins |>
  count(bin_start_g = floor(body_mass_g / 500) * 500)

mass_bins

dir.create(here::here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(mass_bins, here::here("output", "mass_histogram_counts.csv"))
# A tibble: 9 × 2
  bin_start_g     n
        <dbl> <int>
1        2500     9
2        3000    62
3        3500    94
4        4000    59
5        4500    51
6        5000    34
7        5500    29
8        6000     4
9          NA     2

The eight counts add up to 342, and the NA row holds the other 2. These are the heights of the eight bars. Rule 7 of Sandve and colleagues’ ten rules for reproducible research asks for exactly this: keep the counts behind a histogram, not only the picture.

Choosing the bins in code matters for one more reason. The outputs in this book come from ggplot2 3.4.4. ggplot2 4.0.0 changed how it places bins by default, and its own notes say this “may affect plots that use default binning”. A histogram left on defaults can change shape when a colleague runs your script on a newer version. One with its width and boundary written down cannot, unless that version has a bug: the notes for 4.0.1 list a fixed bug in which boundary was ignored.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The bars describe the 342 penguins with a body mass in this file. They are not the shape of body mass in any wider population of penguins.

Another bin width tells a different story. Bins of 100 g show more bumps, and some of them are chance; bins of 1000 g hide real ones. There is no correct width. Try two or three, pick one that shows what the data show, and write it in the code.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now two variables, and the commonest early mistake. Continue in the same session. You want every point blue, and you write the colour inside aes():

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = "blue")) +
  geom_point()
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing missing values (`geom_point()`).

The book prints no picture here, but on your screen the points are not blue. They are ggplot2’s first default colour, a pinkish red, and a legend appears titled “colour” with one entry: “blue”. Inside aes(), “blue” was treated as data, a column whose every value is the word “blue”. ggplot2 gave that one value a colour of its own choosing and explained it in a legend.

Mapping and setting are different acts. Map a colour to a column when you want it to vary with the data. Set it outside aes(), in the geom, when you want one colour for every point:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point()

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(colour = "blue")
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing missing values (`geom_point()`).
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing missing values (`geom_point()`).

The first gives each species its own colour and a legend that means something. The second makes every point blue and needs no legend.

Colour is one way to show a third variable. Facets are another: one small panel per species, on the same axes, so the panels can be compared by eye. Finish the figure as Book 0 asked: axis titles that name the quantity and its unit, and a source line. Then save it from the script, at a size written in the code, into output/.

mass_flipper <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~species) +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    caption = "Source: palmerpenguins raw data, as read from data-raw/"
  )

mass_flipper

dir.create(here::here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  here::here("output", "mass_flipper.png"),
  plot = mass_flipper,
  width = 18,
  height = 10,
  units = "cm"
)

file.exists(here::here("output", "mass_flipper.png"))
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing missing values (`geom_point()`).
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing missing values (`geom_point()`).
[1] TRUE

Three panels, one per species, each on the same scales. ~species reads “by species”. The figure is in output/, made by the same line every time the script runs. The dir.create() line matters for a reader on a newer version: from ggplot2 3.5.0, ggsave() makes a missing folder only when its new create.dir argument tells it to.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
A scatter plot shows that heavier penguins in this file tend to have longer flippers. It does not show that one causes the other, and it says nothing about penguins outside the file.

Facets compare panels well only when they share axes, which facet_wrap() does unless told otherwise. Free axes, one scale per panel, make every panel look equally spread out, and the eye then compares shapes that are drawn on different rulers.

blocks.label: Illustration 3
blocks.html:
Last, the two plots most used in a thesis to compare groups: the boxplot and the bar chart. Continue in the same session.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Body mass (g)")
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing non-finite values (`stat_boxplot()`).

Each box runs from the first quartile to the third, with a line at the median. Which quartiles? The ones quantile() gives, R’s type 7 from the section on summaries; ggplot2’s notes for the newer 4.0.3 name 7 as the default. Check them:

penguins |>
  summarise(
    q1_g = quantile(body_mass_g, probs = 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_g = median(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    q3_g = quantile(body_mass_g, probs = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = species
  )
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  species    q1_g median_g  q3_g
  <chr>     <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 Adelie    3350      3700  4000
2 Gentoo    4700      5000  5500
3 Chinstrap 3488.     3700  3950

The Adelie box runs from 3350 g to 4000 g with its median at 3700 g. The Gentoo box runs from 4700 g to 5500 g. A boxplot’s side axis need not start at zero. Every box, whisker and point carries its value by position, read off the printed scale, as Book 0 said of a line chart.

A bar chart is different. A bar’s value is its length, so its value axis must start at zero. geom_bar() counts the rows in each category, as count() does:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Rows in the file")

On your screen the bars stand at 152, 68 and 124. A bar chart of means, with the axis cut to start at 3000 g, would make the Gentoo bar look about three times the Adelie bar when its mean is about 1.4 times as large. Keep bar charts for counts and amounts that start at zero, and show distributions with boxes or histograms.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
A box hides how many values it summarises: a box drawn from 5 values looks as solid as one drawn from 150. Print the n per group beside the figure, or in its caption.

The 1.4 is rounded: 5076 divided by 3701 is about 1.37. It compares two means in this file and says nothing about how different a typical Gentoo and Adelie are.

points.html: Write a colour or size inside aes() only when it should vary with a column. Inside, a fixed value such as “blue” is treated as data.
Read every message and warning ggplot2 prints. “Removed 2 rows” means your figure shows fewer observations than your data frame holds.
The error is to think a histogram shows the shape of the data. It shows the data cut into bins someone chose.
A bar chart’s value axis starts at zero, because a bar’s value is its length. A boxplot or a scatter plot need not, because position carries the value.
Every axis title names the quantity and its unit, and every figure carries a source line.
Save every figure with ggsave() from the script, with its width, height and units written in.
When a trainee’s thesis figure looks wrong, ask for the code before the picture.
The grammar draws exactly what the code says. It cannot guarantee that the data, the bins or the rows it silently drops are right.

blocks.prompt: Add to your penguin script a histogram of flipper length. Use bins 10 mm wide starting at 170 mm, each including its left edge. Give it an axis title with its unit, and a source line. Save it to output/flipper_histogram.png at 15 cm by 10 cm. Write the counts per bin to output/flipper_histogram_counts.csv. Say how many penguins the figure shows.
blocks.answer:
library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

flipper_plot <- ggplot(penguins_raw, aes(x = `Flipper Length (mm)`)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, boundary = 170, closed = "left") +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Penguins",
    caption = "Source: palmerpenguins raw data, as read from data-raw/"
  )

dir.create(here::here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  here::here("output", "flipper_histogram.png"),
  plot = flipper_plot,
  width = 15,
  height = 10,
  units = "cm"
)

flipper_counts <- penguins_raw |>
  count(bin_start_mm = floor(`Flipper Length (mm)` / 10) * 10)

flipper_counts
write_csv(flipper_counts, here::here("output", "flipper_histogram_counts.csv"))
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing non-finite values (`stat_bin()`).
# A tibble: 8 × 2
  bin_start_mm     n
         <dbl> <int>
1          170     8
2          180    69
3          190   113
4          200    38
5          210    71
6          220    35
7          230     8
8           NA     2

The warning says 2 rows were removed, so the figure shows 342 rows. The counts per bin are in the CSV file, beside the figure they describe; the NA row holds the 2 with no flipper length.

blocks.prompt: A colleague makes the figures for her thesis by running code in the console. Then she clicks Export in RStudio’s plot pane and chooses “Save as image”. She drags the size until it looks right. After a data correction, she has to remake eleven figures. Say what is wrong with this way of working and what she should do.
blocks.answer:
Nothing connects each saved image to the code and data that made it. The console keeps no record of which lines made figure 7, and the size she dragged to is written nowhere. After a correction she must remember, for each of eleven figures, which code made it and at what size, and get all of them right by hand.

Instead, put every figure in the analysis script. Make it with ggplot() and give it a name. Then save it with ggsave() into output/, with its file name, width, height and units in the code. After a correction she reruns the script once. All eleven figures are redrawn from the corrected data, at the same size. Keep the counts behind each figure in a file beside it, so a reader can check the numbers without measuring the picture.

blocks.prompt: A journalist has three minutes. She has a bar chart from a press release. One district’s bar for “adults screened” looks five times another’s, and the axis starts at 9,000. Explain what she should ask for, without jargon.
blocks.answer: “A bar is read by its length, so the bars only tell the truth if they start at zero. This axis starts at 9,000, so the bottom of every bar has been cut off. A district with 10,000 adults screened and one with 9,200 would look like a tall bar and a stub, even though the numbers are close. Ask for the chart redrawn from zero, or simply ask for the numbers. If the press office made the chart in code, redrawing it is one line.”

blocks.prompt: Without looking back, name the three parts of a ggplot2 plot, and two choices that change a histogram’s bars without changing the data.
blocks.answer:
The data, the aesthetic mappings made with aes(), and the geom.

The bin width and where the bins start (binwidth and boundary). Which edge each bin includes (closed) changes the bars too, when values sit exactly on edges.

blocks.prompt:
In this line, name the data, each aesthetic mapping, and the geom.

ggplot(clinic, aes(x = age_years, y = bmi)) + geom_point()
blocks.answer: The data are clinic. There are two mappings: age_years to position along x, and bmi to position along y. The geom is geom_point(), so each row becomes one point. The line draws a scatter plot of BMI against age.

blocks.prompt:
In each line, say whether the colour is mapped or set, and what the points will look like.

ggplot(clinic, aes(x = age_years, y = bmi, colour = sex)) + geom_point()
ggplot(clinic, aes(x = age_years, y = bmi)) + geom_point(colour = "darkgreen")
blocks.answer:
In the first, colour is mapped to the column sex, inside aes(). Each value of sex gets its own colour, and a legend says which is which.

In the second, colour is set, outside aes(). Every point is dark green, and there is no legend, because nothing varies.

blocks.prompt: Six made-up values: 1.2, 1.8, 2.1, 2.9, 3.0 and 3.4. A histogram uses binwidth = 1 and boundary = 1, with ggplot2’s default for which edge a bin includes. How many values go in the bins from 1 to 2, 2 to 3 and 3 to 4? Then answer again with closed = "left".
blocks.answer:
By default a bin includes its right edge. The first bin is “above 1, up to 2”, and the others follow the same pattern. The first holds 1.2 and 1.8: 2 values. The second holds 2.1, 2.9 and 3.0: 3 values. The third holds 3.4 alone: 1 value.

With closed = "left" the bins are “1 up to under 2”, “2 up to under 3” and “3 up to 4”. The first holds 1.2 and 1.8: 2 values. The second holds 2.1 and 2.9: 2 values. The value 3.0 moves to the third, with 3.4: 2 values.

Only the value sitting exactly on an edge moved. In real data, measurements are often rounded to whole numbers, so many values sit on edges, and the choice changes the bars.

blocks.prompt:
Read the penguin file.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Draw a boxplot of body mass by island, with axis titles. Then give the median and the quartiles the boxes are drawn from, with the number of body masses behind each box.
blocks.answer:
ggplot(penguins_raw, aes(x = Island, y = `Body Mass (g)`)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Island", y = "Body mass (g)")

penguins_raw |>
  summarise(
    n_mass = sum(!is.na(`Body Mass (g)`)),
    q1_g = quantile(`Body Mass (g)`, probs = 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_g = median(`Body Mass (g)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    q3_g = quantile(`Body Mass (g)`, probs = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = Island
  )
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing non-finite values (`stat_boxplot()`).
# A tibble: 3 × 5
  Island    n_mass  q1_g median_g  q3_g
  <chr>      <int> <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 Torgersen     51 3338.    3700  4000
2 Biscoe       167 4200     4775  5325
3 Dream        124 3400     3688. 3956.

The warning says 2 rows were removed: two penguins with no body mass. Biscoe’s box sits highest, with a median of 4775 g from 167 body masses. The boxes use the same quartiles as quantile(). Biscoe is the only island with Gentoo penguins, the heaviest species, so the island comparison is partly a species comparison.

blocks.prompt:
Read the penguin file.

library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Draw a scatter plot of culmen depth against culmen length, one panel per species. The culmen is the ridge of the bill. Give axis titles that carry units, and a source line. Save it to output/culmen.png at 18 cm by 8 cm, and show that the file exists.
blocks.answer:
culmen_plot <- ggplot(
  penguins_raw,
  aes(x = `Culmen Length (mm)`, y = `Culmen Depth (mm)`)
) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~Species) +
  labs(
    x = "Culmen length (mm)",
    y = "Culmen depth (mm)",
    caption = "Source: palmerpenguins raw data, as read from data-raw/"
  )

dir.create(here::here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  here::here("output", "culmen.png"),
  plot = culmen_plot,
  width = 18,
  height = 8,
  units = "cm"
)

file.exists(here::here("output", "culmen.png"))
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing missing values (`geom_point()`).
[1] TRUE

The file exists. The plot was never shown on the screen, but ggsave() drew it to make the file. Its warning says 2 rows were removed: the penguins with no culmen measurements are not in the saved figure. Say so in the caption if the figure goes in a report.

blocks.prompt:
Read the penguin file.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Draw a bar chart of the number of rows for each value of Sex, with axis titles. Give the heights of the bars, and say what the third bar is.
blocks.answer:
ggplot(penguins_raw, aes(x = Sex)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Sex as recorded", y = "Rows in the file")

penguins_raw |>
  count(Sex)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Sex        n
  <chr>  <int>
1 FEMALE   165
2 MALE     168
3 <NA>      11

165 female, 168 male, and 11 with no sex recorded. The NA rows get a bar of their own, just as count() gives them a row of their own. Keep it: the reader should see that 11 penguins could not be put in either group. The bars start at zero, so their lengths compare fairly.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague wants all points dark red, and writes:

ggplot(penguins_raw, aes(x = `Flipper Length (mm)`, y = `Body Mass (g)`, colour = "darkred")) +
  geom_point()

The points come out pinkish red, and a legend says “darkred”. She decides her version of R “cannot show dark red”. Find what broke.
blocks.answer:
The colour is inside aes(), so it is a mapping. ggplot2 treated “darkred” as a value in the data, a column holding that one word, and gave it the first colour of its own default set. The legend explains that value. R can draw dark red; it was never asked to.

Move the colour out of aes(), into the geom, to set it:

ggplot(penguins_raw, aes(x = `Flipper Length (mm)`, y = `Body Mass (g)`)) +
  geom_point(colour = "darkred")

Why the wrong conclusion looks reasonable: the code contains the word “darkred” and produced a colour close to it. So the gap looks like a limit of the software. The legend is the clue: a legend appears only for something mapped.

blocks.prompt: You and a colleague run the same script on the same penguin file. Your histogram of body mass, made with geom_histogram() and no other arguments, has a different shape from hers. You have ggplot2 3.4.4; she has 4.0.3. She concludes one of the two data files must be corrupt. Say what is more likely, and how to make the two figures agree.
blocks.answer:
The data are more likely the same, and the bins different. ggplot2’s notes for version 4.0.0 say the default bin boundary changed, and that this “may affect plots that use default binning”. With no binwidth or boundary given, each version placed its 30 bins its own way.

Check the data first, cheaply: compare row counts and a checksum of the raw file, as the section on raw files taught. Then make the bins part of the code:

ggplot(penguins_raw, aes(x = `Body Mass (g)`)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 500, boundary = 2500, closed = "left")

With the width, the boundary and the edge rule written down, both versions draw the same bins. Why the wrong conclusion looks reasonable: the code and the file are the same, so a different picture seems to mean different data. The third ingredient, the package version, is invisible unless you print it.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague used to the pipe writes:

library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
ggplot(penguins_raw, aes(x = `Flipper Length (mm)`, y = `Body Mass (g)`)) |>
  geom_point()
Error in `geom_point()`:
! `mapping` must be created by `aes()`
ℹ Did you use `%>%` or `|>` instead of `+`?

Read the error. Say what broke and fix it.
blocks.answer:
Layers are added to a plot with +, not passed along with |>. The pipe handed the whole plot to geom_point() as its first argument, where geom_point() expects a mapping. The error message even asks whether you used |> instead of +.

ggplot(penguins_raw, aes(x = `Flipper Length (mm)`, y = `Body Mass (g)`)) +
  geom_point()
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing missing values (`geom_point()`).

Now the plot draws, with the usual warning about 2 rows removed.

Why the wrong code looks reasonable: in every section before this one, each step of the work was joined to the next with |>. ggplot2 is older than that habit and builds a plot by adding layers.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up thesis figure caption says: “Figure 3. Body mass of all 344 penguins, by species.” The code was:

library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

ggplot(penguins_raw, aes(x = Species, y = `Body Mass (g)`)) +
  geom_boxplot()
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing non-finite values (`stat_boxplot()`).

Find what is wrong with the caption, using only what R printed.
blocks.answer:
R printed a warning: 2 rows were removed. The boxes are drawn from 342 body masses, not 344. Two penguins have no body mass, and geom_boxplot() left them out. The caption should say 342, and the methods should say why 2 are missing.

Count them to be sure:

sum(is.na(penguins_raw$`Body Mass (g)`))
[1] 2

Why the wrong caption looks reasonable: 344 is the number of rows in the file, which everyone remembers. A warning in the console is easy to scroll past, and it is the only place the difference is shown.

blocks.prompt: A made-up draft says: “As Figure 1 shows, most penguins weigh between 3.5 and 4 kg.” Draw the histogram that would back the claim, and count the penguins in that range. Say whether the claim holds, and what the figure does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Draw the histogram with bins 500 g wide starting at 2500 g, so one bar is exactly 3500 to under 4000 g, and count:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

ggplot(penguins_raw, aes(x = `Body Mass (g)`)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 500, boundary = 2500, closed = "left")

penguins_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(`Body Mass (g)`)) |>
  summarise(
    n_mass = n(),
    n_3500_to_4000 = sum(`Body Mass (g)` >= 3500 & `Body Mass (g)` < 4000),
    pct = 100 * n_3500_to_4000 / n_mass
  )
Warning message:
Removed 2 rows containing non-finite values (`stat_bin()`).
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  n_mass n_3500_to_4000   pct
   <int>          <int> <dbl>
1    342             94  27.5

94 of the 342 penguins with a body mass, 27.5%, weigh from 3500 g to under 4000 g. That bar is the tallest, so 3.5 to 4 kg is the commonest band. But “most” means more than half, and this is about a quarter. The sentence should say “the commonest band was 3.5 to 4 kg, holding 94 of 342 penguins (27.5%)”.

What the figure does not establish:

  • That the commonest band would be the same with other bins. With 250 g bins the tallest bar could move.
  • Anything about a typical penguin of any one species. The histogram mixes three species of different size.
  • Anything about penguins outside this study.

blocks.prompt: A made-up district officer says: “Give me one figure comparing BMI in men and women from that American survey, for my slides.” Make it from the joined NHANES files for adults aged 20 or over, save it to output/, and say what the figure does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Join the files and keep the adults. Label the codes: the codebook says RIAGENDR 1 is male and 2 is female. Draw boxes rather than bars, since BMI is a distribution and does not start at zero:

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)

bmx <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "BMX_L.xpt"))
demo <- haven::read_xpt(here::here("data-raw", "DEMO_L.xpt"))

adults <- bmx |>
  left_join(demo, by = "SEQN", relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20, !is.na(BMXBMI)) |>
  mutate(sex = if_else(RIAGENDR == 1, "Men", "Women"))

count(adults, sex)

bmi_plot <- ggplot(adults, aes(x = sex, y = BMXBMI)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "BMI (kg/m^2)",
    caption = "NHANES 2021-2023, examined adults aged 20 or over; unweighted, not a US estimate"
  )

dir.create(here::here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(
  here::here("output", "nhanes_bmi_by_sex.png"),
  plot = bmi_plot,
  width = 12,
  height = 10,
  units = "cm"
)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sex       n
  <chr> <int>
1 Men    2680
2 Women  3290

The figure has two boxes, from 2680 men and 3290 women with a BMI. The rows with no BMI were removed before plotting, on purpose, so the counts printed are the counts drawn. NULL leaves that axis without a title. The caption says what the boxes are, and what they are not.

What it does not establish:

  • Anything about adults in the United States. The boxes are unweighted; the survey’s documentation says its sample weights should be used.
  • Whether the difference between the boxes is more than chance, or large enough to matter.
  • Anything about adults in the officer’s district. A figure from one country’s survey is not a figure for another country’s people.
  • A clean comparison of BMI. It includes women who were pregnant at the exam, whose weight does not measure the same thing.
